input.topic: Two friends at a railway station discover their tickets are for different destinations.
input.recentProse:
Анна и Иван на вокзале. У Анны маленькая сумка. У Ивана большой рюкзак. Друзья стоят рядом и ждут поезд.

Анна достаёт билет.

— У меня есть билет. Я еду в Москву, — говорит Анна.

Иван тоже достаёт билет.

— У меня есть билет. Я еду в Казань, — говорит Иван.

Анна смотрит на Ивана.

— В Казань? Но мы едем вместе!

— Да, вместе, в Москву, — говорит Иван.

Иван смотрит на свой билет ещё раз. На билете слово «Казань».

Анна показывает свой билет. На её билете слово «Москва».

— У нас разные билеты, — говорит Анна. — Я еду в Москву, а ты едешь в Казань.

— Да. Это разные города, — говорит Иван.

Рядом стоит поезд. Иван смотрит на поезд, потом на Анну.

— Анна, что мы теперь делаем?

Woman; here, the woman working at the ticket counter.
Hello; a polite greeting used with a stranger.
I; the person speaking.
To want. Хочу means 'I want'; хотим means 'we want.' Followed here by an infinitive.
To travel by transport; here, to go by train. An imperfective infinitive after 'want.'
But; introduces the problem with Ivan’s ticket.
I have; literally, 'with me.' Меня is the genitive form of я. Есть can be omitted, as in у меня билет.
Ticket. Билет is singular; билета is used after два; билетов is genitive plural after нет.
To look at something or someone. На is followed here by the accusative case.
Yes; confirms what destination the ticket is for.
This or it, used to identify something: 'this is a ticket.' Russian does not need a present-tense word for 'is' here.
She; refers to the woman at the counter.
We; refers to the two friends together.
Together; travelling with one another.
Also or too; shows that Anna does the same thing or has the same wish.
Screen; here, the screen the woman checks.
There is or there are; also used in questions about having something available.
Another or a different one; describes an alternative train.
Train.
He or it; here, 'it' refers to поезд, a masculine noun.
In the evening; tells when the train runs and when the friends can travel.
And, but, or 'what about'; here, introduces a question about an alternative train or the other person.
This; points to the particular train already being discussed. Masculine singular to match поезд.
To ask a question. Спрашивает means 'asks.'
For this train; describes which train the tickets would be for.
There is none or there are none. Билетов нет means 'there are no tickets'; the noun uses the genitive case.
To be able to or can. Могу means 'I can' and is followed by an infinitive.
To go or set off by transport. A perfective infinitive, referring here to a planned train journey.
You, when speaking informally to one person.
What about you? A short question asking whether the other person can do the same.
To put or place something down. Кладёт means 'puts.'
One’s own; here, Anna’s own ticket. Agrees with the masculine noun билет.
Onto the table; на takes the accusative case for where something is being placed.
Table or desk; here, the surface where Anna puts her ticket.
Do you have? Here, вас is the polite form of 'you,' addressed to the woman.
Two. Before a masculine noun, два is followed by the genitive singular: два билета.
Again; the woman checks the screen another time.
And; joins the two friends’ names.
To wait. Ждут means 'they are waiting.'
At or by the ticket counter. У takes the genitive case.
